periods.analysis: Fleet uptime finished 2024-Q3 at 94.3%, green against the >=92.0% target; this is our baseline in this run, so there is no prior quarter movement to report. The shop kept the summer construction and beach-route load under control by holding two preventive-maintenance lanes open for dump trucks and refuse packers, with Fleet Tech Crew B focused on heavy units PW-412 through PW-427. The misses were not mysterious: three aerial-lift trucks waited on hydraulic hose kits, and two police interceptors sat for camera upfit wiring. Overall, the equipment was available when crews needed it, which is the point of the measure, not a trophy for the wall.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the 500-hour PM block protected on Tuesdays and Thursdays and not using it as overflow for cosmetic repairs. Extend the parts-bin pilot for hydraulic hoses and brake wear kits to the sanitation and streets cohorts before leaf season starts. I also want the weekly ClearPoint note to list any unit down more than 5 business days by asset ID, so the budget ask stays tied to evidence instead of anecdotes.

periods.analysis: Fleet uptime was 93.4% in 2024-Q4, down 0.9 points from 94.3% but still green and still above the 92.0% target. The dip is consistent with winterization, plow spreader installs, and year-end inspections hitting the same shop calendar; that is not a surprise, but it is still shop time. Units PW-118, PW-203, and SW-071 each lost days waiting on alternators from the regional vendor, and those small delays add up. The important part is that the refuse, police, fire support, and road-response fleets stayed available for service, even with holiday staffing.
periods.recommendations: Keep the winter make-ready checklist, but start it two weeks earlier next year for spreader controllers and battery load tests. Put alternators, DEF sensors, and light-bar harnesses on a minimum/maximum inventory level at Central Shop, because the vendor lead time is no longer a theory. Maintain the green by continuing Friday morning triage with Operations, so low-priority body work does not occupy bays needed for mission units.

periods.analysis: Fleet uptime improved to 94.8% in 2025-Q1, up 1.4 points from 93.4%, which puts us comfortably green. The earlier parts staging and the winter PM list did what they were supposed to do: fewer trucks sat waiting for $80 parts while $250,000 assets were idle. Crew A cleared the backlog on snow-response units PW-201 through PW-219 after the January storms, and the new diagnostic tablet cut repeat visits on the Ford interceptor cohort. This is a good example of boring maintenance paying for itself, which is still my favorite kind.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the gain by making the diagnostic tablet workflow standard for police and inspection vehicles, with fault codes attached to each work order. Extend the winter parts minimums into a formal critical-spares list before the FY2026 budget lock, including quantities and actual usage. Keep measuring downtime by asset class, because one average number can hide a weak cohort.

periods.analysis: Fleet uptime reached 96.2% in 2025-Q2, up another 1.4 points from 94.8%, the strongest quarter in this sequence and green by a healthy margin. The spring changeover went cleanly because Streets, Parks, and Utilities staggered their equipment releases instead of all showing up at Bay 3 on the same Monday. We also saw fewer repeat failures after replacing cooling-system components on mowers PK-034 through PK-049 and vac trucks UT-506 and UT-508 before peak heat. That is the kind of asset-condition work that does not look exciting until crews are not waiting in the yard.
periods.recommendations: Do not treat 96.2% as permission to coast; use it to document what worked. Lock in the staggered release calendar with Streets, Parks, Utilities, and Police for every seasonal transition. Extend the cooling-system pre-check to the refuse packer cohort before July, and include radiator pressure-test results in the work-order closeout.

periods.analysis: Fleet uptime settled to 94.9% in 2025-Q3, down 1.3 points from 96.2% but still green and still above target. The movement is reasonable given summer paving support, beach enforcement, and the higher mileage on light-duty inspection vehicles during the permit surge along Shoreline Drive. We had concentrated downtime in three tandem dump trucks, PW-414, PW-419, and PW-423, tied to suspension and tire wear after hauling millings. The system is holding, but the quarter reminds us that high utilization consumes steel, rubber, and patience.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by keeping the tire and suspension inspection at every 250-hour interval for the heavy dump cohort through paving season. Extend the route-based mileage review to building inspection and code enforcement vehicles, since those units are now acting like high-mileage service vehicles, not office cars. Bring the PW-414/PW-419/PW-423 repair history to the capital replacement ranking meeting, with downtime days and parts cost included.

periods.analysis: Fleet uptime was 94.6% in 2025-Q4, down 0.3 points from 94.9%, which is a small decline and still green. The shop absorbed year-end emissions inspections, plow mounting, and several warranty campaigns without losing control of the availability number. The main watch item was vendor turnaround on diesel particulate filter cleaning for refuse units RF-221 through RF-226; the equipment came back, but not fast. Compared with last year’s Q4 at 93.4%, the fleet is in better condition and the work planning is cleaner.
periods.recommendations: Keep the plow and winterization schedule exactly as a gated checklist, with no unit released until batteries, hydraulics, lights, and spreader controls are signed off. Extend the DPF cleaning contract to include a 72-hour turnaround clause or an exchange-core option for the refuse cohort. Continue the capital replacement evidence file for units that cross both 10 years and 20 downtime days, because that is how we defend the ask.

periods.analysis: Fleet uptime improved to 95.6% in 2026-Q1, up 1.0 point from 94.6%, and remains green. The winter was not especially kind, but the fleet was ready: pre-staged plow parts, battery testing, and the new DPF turnaround language all reduced avoidable downtime. Crew B also separated quick-turn light-duty work from heavy repairs, so a sedan oil leak did not block a bay needed for a loader or plow truck. The number tells the same story the crews told me: fewer surprises, faster returns to service.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 95.6% level by preserving the quick-turn lane for jobs under 2 labor hours and tracking whether it stays under that limit. Extend the DPF contract approach to hydraulic-cylinder rebuilds for loaders LD-302 and LD-305 and backhoes BH-117 through BH-121. Use the Q1 work-order data to update replacement scores before budget hearings, not after the fleet has already made the argument for us.

periods.analysis: Fleet uptime closed 2026-Q2 at 95.1%, down 0.5 points from 95.6% but still clearly green. The modest decline came during spring construction startup, parks mowing, and higher utility-call volume, so some wear was expected. The shop kept control by rotating PM slots around the Harborview Avenue resurfacing support fleet and by moving mower blade and spindle work to the Parks satellite bay instead of Central Shop. We are not at the 2025-Q2 peak of 96.2%, but the two-year arc shows a reliable fleet program, not a lucky quarter.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by keeping satellite maintenance for Parks equipment during mowing season and measuring whether it reduces transport downtime. Extend the construction-season PM rotation to any unit assigned more than 30 hours per week to paving, striping, or utility restoration support. For the next quarter, watch heavy-unit tire wear and parts lead times by asset ID, because that is where a good uptime number can start leaking.

periods.analysis: Illustrative September import: fleet uptime was 94.4%, above the 92% target but down from 95.1% in June. The fleet remains available for utility and street work; the downward movement warrants a maintenance check.
periods.recommendations: Review heavy-unit parts delays and preventive-maintenance slots before winter response demand increases.
